title: Explain human resource policies and procedures

lessons.title: HR policies on the farm and the law behind them
lessons.html:
Policies and procedures

A policy is a farm rule or principle, for example "All workers must wear PPE when spraying." A procedure explains the steps to follow, for example how to apply for leave. Together they make sure everyone is treated fairly and consistently and that the farm obeys the law.

Main South African labour laws

  • Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 (BCEA): working hours, overtime, leave, payslips, notice periods.
  • Sectoral Determination for Farm Workers: applies BCEA rules to the agricultural sector.
  • National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018: the national minimum wage, which is updated regularly; check the current rate.
  • Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 (LRA): fair dismissal, disputes, unions and the CCMA.
  • Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998: no unfair discrimination.
  • Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993: a safe workplace.
  • Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 (COIDA): compensation for injuries at work.
  • Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001: UIF contributions and benefits.

Typical farm HR policies

  • Recruitment and selection
  • Contracts of employment and job descriptions
  • Working hours, overtime and rest days
  • Leave: annual, sick, family responsibility and maternity
  • Remuneration and deductions
  • Health and safety, including PPE and incident reporting
  • Disciplinary code and procedure
  • Grievance procedure
  • Housing, transport and alcohol and drug rules where relevant
  • Harassment and anti-discrimination

Every worker should have a written contract and access to the policies in a language they understand. Supervisors must know the policies well enough to explain them and apply them consistently.

lessons.title: Applying key procedures as a supervisor
lessons.html:
Your role

Supervisors are often the first point of contact for workers. You apply procedures day to day and pass issues to management or HR when needed.

Leave procedure

  1. Worker applies on the leave form, in advance for annual leave.
  2. Supervisor checks work plans and recommends.
  3. Manager approves; the record is updated.
  4. For sick leave, a medical certificate may be required as set out in the BCEA and farm policy.

Grievance procedure

A grievance is a complaint by a worker about treatment at work.

  1. The worker raises it with the supervisor, verbally or in writing.
  2. The supervisor listens, records it and tries to resolve it within the set time.
  3. If not resolved, it goes to the next level of management.
  4. If still unresolved, it may be referred externally, such as to the CCMA, depending on the issue.

Never victimise a worker for raising a grievance.

Disciplinary procedure

Discipline aims to correct behaviour, not punish. It must be fair in substance (there was a valid rule, the worker knew it and broke it) and in procedure.

  • Minor issues: verbal warning, then written warning, then final written warning.
  • Serious misconduct (e.g. theft, assault, being drunk while operating machinery): may lead to a hearing and possible dismissal.
  • The worker must be told the charge, given time to prepare, allowed a representative and allowed to state their side.
  • Keep written records of every step.

Incident and injury reporting

Report every injury immediately so first aid is given and the incident is recorded for COIDA and OHS purposes.

Good practice

  • Treat everyone consistently.
  • Keep personal information confidential.
  • Ask HR or management when unsure.

Key points

  • Policies are rules; procedures are the steps to follow.
  • Farm HR policies must comply with the BCEA, LRA, OHS Act and other labour laws.
  • Grievances must be heard and never punished.
  • Discipline must be fair in substance and procedure, with records.
  • Supervisors apply procedures consistently and escalate when unsure.
